title: Phones at School: Less Learning, More Loneliness
author: Jean M. Twenge
summary: Twenge presents new PISA-based analysis across 36 countries showing that where 15-16 year-olds spend more time on devices for leisure during the school day, standardized scores in math, reading, and science declined more sharply from 2012 to 2022 and school-based loneliness rose more steeply. She pairs that with U.S. data indicating teens spend over an hour per school day on phones almost entirely for non-educational use, amounting to roughly 20% of school time off-task. The article's policy conclusion is bell-to-bell restriction, not just class-time bans, because the lunchroom and passing periods are where peer connection is being displaced. She extends the frame to school-issued laptops and tablets, which often remain open to YouTube and streaming, and flags paper-and-pencil as a plausible default for younger grades. Her operational claim is that the twin outcomes (lower achievement and more loneliness) are not coincidences but two sides of the same device-displacement effect.
points: The PISA data supplies cross-country evidence: where leisure device use during school is high, both test-score decline and loneliness rose more steeply over 2012-2022, holding GDP per capita constant.
Policy ask is bell-to-bell, not just classroom-only: lunch and passing periods are where the social fabric forms, and that is where phones do the most displacement damage.
School-issued laptops are the next front. Many permit YouTube and streaming, which undermines the gains from phone bans.
The twin outcomes (academic decline and loneliness) are the same effect viewed from different angles, not separate problems to solve in parallel.
A 20% off-task share is the right scale to frame the argument: this is not a minor distraction, it is one-fifth of the instructional week.
quotes: A recent analysis found that American teens spend more than an hour using their phones during the school day, and almost none of that time is spent on educational activities.
Electronic devices are both distracting in the classroom and isolating in the lunchroom.

In countries where students spent a lot of time using devices for leisure during the school day, test scores plummeted between 2012 and 2022. In countries where they spent less time, test scores merely slid.
These results show the twin impacts of the leisure use of devices during the school day: Declines in test scores and increases in feeling lonely at school.
Schools should restrict students' use of smartphones from bell to bell, not just during class, but also during lunch, breaks, and passing periods.
The next step is to lock down laptops and tablets so they, too, aren't being used for social media and entertainment during the school day.
Sticking with the status quo means lower test scores and more lonely students, not the outcome any of us want.” Archived from Generation Tech (Substack) on April 21, 2026 by Tim.
